questions.question: Compare the Waterfall and Agile process models.
questions.answer: Waterfall runs phases in a fixed order (requirements → design → build → test) and suits stable requirements, but problems surface late. Agile delivers in short iterations with continuous customer feedback, so it handles changing requirements well.

questions.question: What is the difference between verification and validation?
questions.answer: Verification: “are we building the product right?” — reviews, walkthroughs and inspections against the specification. Validation: “are we building the right product?” — testing the working software against user needs.

questions.question: Explain coupling and cohesion. Which should be high?
questions.answer: Cohesion is how closely related a module’s responsibilities are — aim for high. Coupling is how much modules depend on each other — aim for low. High cohesion and low coupling make code easier to change and test.

questions.question: State the Master theorem and solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.
questions.answer: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). Here a = 2, b = 2, so n^(log₂2) = n, which matches f(n). That is case 2, giving T(n) = Θ(n log n).

questions.question: Greedy vs dynamic programming — when does each work?
questions.answer: Greedy works when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure; it makes one choice per step (e.g. activity selection). DP works when subproblems overlap; it stores sub-results to avoid recomputation (e.g. 0/1 knapsack).

questions.question: Why does Dijkstra’s algorithm fail with negative edge weights?
questions.answer: It finalises a vertex as soon as it is removed from the queue, assuming no later path can be shorter. A negative edge can break that assumption. Bellman–Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.

questions.question: Explain the four rotations used to rebalance an AVL tree.
questions.answer: LL case → single right rotation. RR case → single left rotation. LR case → left rotation on the child, then right rotation. RL case → right rotation on the child, then left rotation. Afterwards every balance factor is −1, 0 or +1.

questions.question: How does a hash table handle collisions?
questions.answer: Separate chaining keeps a list at each slot. Open addressing finds another slot by linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing. Keeping the load factor low keeps average lookups close to O(1).
